subject: business-studies
title: Liquidity Ratios
welcome_lead: Can the firm pay its bills next month? Liquidity ratios answer.
meta_desc: A-Level Ratio Analysis: current ratio and acid test.
final_note: Liquidity ratios reveal short-term survival risk in seconds.

concepts.def: Stock, debtors, cash - convertible within a year.
Inventory of raw materials, work in progress and finished goods.

walkthroughs.body_html: Current ratio = CA / CL. A retailer with high stock can show 2.0 yet still be tight on cash. Acid test = (CA - stock) / CL strips out the less-liquid item.
A current ratio around 1.5 to 2 is comfortable for most industries. Below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets - distress likely. Above 3 suggests idle cash.
To raise the current ratio: sell slow-moving stock, chase debtors, renegotiate supplier credit. Each move has a cost - discounted stock sales, factoring fees, lost discounts.

mcqs.q: Acid test ratio strips out which item?
options: Cash
Stock
Debtors
Creditors

mcqs.q: A current ratio below 1 usually signals:
options: Excess liquidity
Liquidity stress
Strong profitability
Low gearing

mcqs.q: What does a liquidity ratio like the current ratio measure?
options: A business's ability to meet short-term obligations — current assets divided by current liabilities. A ratio above 1 means assets cover liabilities; too high may indicate poor use of resources.
Liquidity ratios measure how quickly a business sells products.
A higher liquidity ratio is always better.
Break-even is where the business owes no debt.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
Break-even is where the business makes the most profit.
Break-even is where the business owes no debt.
The level of output where total revenue equals total costs — neither profit nor loss. It is NOT the level where profit is maximised; profit grows beyond break-even.

mcqs.q: Why are cash flow and profit different on different time-scales?
options: Profit is recognised when a sale is made (even on credit); cash flow is when money actually moves. A profitable sale today may produce no cash for 60 days while bills are due — creating a cash-flow problem despite profit.
Cash flow and profit are the same thing measured differently.
Break-even is where the business owes no debt.
Cash flow only matters at year-end.
